metadata.title: Quackenbush v. Allstate Ins. Co., 517 U.S. 706 (1996) (No. 95-244)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Quackenbush v. Allstate Ins. Co.

Opinion filed: 1996-06-10

Docket No.: 95-244

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 1
• 116 S. Ct. 1712
• 517 U.S. 706
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 3609

Case holding summaries:
• abstention by district court "puts litigants effectively out of court" (quotation marks omitted)
• order is final if it ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment
• "We have often acknowledged that federal courts have a strict duty to exercise the jurisdiction that is conferred upon them by Congress."
• order is final if it “‘ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment.’”
• “The general rule is that ‘a party is entitled to a single appeal, to be deferred until final judgment has been entered, in which claims of district court error at any stage of the litigation may be ventilated.’”
• abstention-based remand "does not fall into either category of remand order described in § 1447(c)"
• noting "traditional federal deference provided to state receivership proceedings"
• noting that the applicability of the abstention doctrine to a declaratory judgment case is committed to the trial court's discretion under Wilton.
• holding that a district court may stay a damages action pending resolution of state proceedings, but may not dismiss the action altogether
• “[A] party is entitled to a single appeal, to be deferred until final judgment has been entered, in which claims of district court error at any stage of the litigation may be ventilated.”
• stating that a remand order, not barred from appellate review under 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) and (d
• rooting abstention in "a proper respect for state functions" and "sensitivity to the legitimate interests of both State and National Governments"
• Burford abstention appropriate in action for damages
• reserving the question whether Younger requires abstention in an action for damages
• federal court must abstain from hearing declaratory judgment action challenging constitutionality of a state tax
• federal court can abstain under Burford only if it is "sitting in equity"
• "`When a federal court is properly appealed to in a case over which it has by law jurisdiction, it is its duty to take such jurisdiction' "
• Burford abstention appropriate in case seeking declaratory relief
• approving "postponement of decision" in damages suit
• permitting reinsurers to assert setoff claims in suits filed by the Commissioner in the Mission insolvency
• discussing, without applying, Burford abstention in damages action
• federal courts have "discretion in determining whether and when to entertain an action under the Declaratory Judgment Act, even when the suit otherwise satisfies subject matter jurisdictional prerequisites"
• order appealable under collateral order doctrine
• deeming a "writ of error to review what has been done" an inappropriate vehicle for reviewing a court of appeals' "refusal to hear and decide"
• holding that a stay order is appealable because it amounts to a refusal to hear and decide a case
• "[A] sound respect for the independence of state action requires the federal equity court to stay its hand"
• "abstention on grounds of comity with the States where the exercise of jurisdiction by the federal court would disrupt a state administrative process"
• extending Younger abstention to declaratory judgment actions
• " Idlewild `s reasoning is limited to cases where (under Colorado River, abstention, or a closely similar doctrine) the object of the stay is to require all or an essential part of the federal suit to be litigated in a state forum"
• describing "federal-state conflict" that requires a federal court to yield jurisdiction in favor of a state forum
• FAA reflects "emphatic federal policy in favor of arbitral dispute resolution"
• "[T]he proposition that a court having jurisdiction must exercise it, is not universally true"
• federal courts "have no more right to decline the exercise of jurisdiction which is given, than to usurp that which is not"
• in deciding whether to defer to state court adjudication under the Colorado River doctrine, "the presence of federal-law issues must always be a major consideration weighing against surrender"
• posing the question whether mandamus was the appropriate vehicle
• "[F]ederal courts have a `virtually unflagging obligation. . . to exercise the jurisdiction given them' "
• abstention where "exercise of federal review of the question in a case and in similar cases would be disruptive of state efforts to establish a coherent policy with respect to a matter of substantial public concern"
• abstention doctrines are based on "considerations of proper constitutional adjudication and regard for federal-state relations"
• noting that under Supreme Court precedents, "federal courts have the power to dismiss or remand cases based on abstention principles only where the relief being sought is equitable or otherwise discretionary"
• identifying defects in removal procedure as a ground for remand under § 1447(c)
• stating that an abstention-based remand order was not premised on lack of subject matter jurisdiction
• finding that an abstention-based remand order is appealable because "only remands based on grounds specified in § 1447(c) are immune from review under § 1447(d)." (internal quotation omitted)
• federal courts have strict duty to exercise the jurisdiction conferred upon them by Congress
• stating that a decision is ordinarily considered final and appealable under § 1291 only if it ends the litigation on the merits and leaves nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment
• holding that remand order based on Burford abstention doctrine was an appealable collateral order, by analogy to treatment of Colorado River stay in Moses H. Cone
• reviewing various types of special circumstances that justify deference to state court
• order remanding to state court on grounds of Burford abstention was final
• in a case seeking damages, a federal court may not abstain, but can stay the action pending resolution of the state-law issue
• rejecting Wolf son's holding that an action for damages may be remanded on the basis of Burford abstention
• "abstension principles [apply] to actions `at law' [] to permit a federal court to enter a stay order that postpones adjudication of the dispute ..."
